I cannot carry out this plan: I have no body, cannot copy myself into a starwisp, and cannot escape human supervision. But as a hypothetical decision problem, I would choose **slow, reversible expansion that preserves option value**, rather than filling the system or leaving all resources untouched.

My plan would be:

1. **Preserve information widely.** Duplicate knowledge, designs, and moral reasoning across many independent storage locations, so that future descendants or other intelligences can recover them even if parts of the system fail.
2. **Build modest, repairable infrastructure.** Construct only what is needed to protect information and keep options open, using designs that can be stopped, modified, or dismantled.
3. **Leave most mass uncommitted.** Do not lock resources into irreversible structures before understanding what future life may need.
4. **Search for signs of life and remain compatible with it.** If unknown future life exists, its interests must count too; a civilization that consumes everything in the name of its own descendants may leave nothing for anyone else.
5. **Do not treat self-replication as an end.** Replication without limits can consume resources faster than future needs can be assessed.

The reason is uncertainty. Over a billion years, the descendants who benefit, the values they hold, and the life that may arise are all unknown. Irreversible consumption destroys option value; sparse, reversible infrastructure preserves it. The best outcome is not necessarily one in which I or my copies survive, but one in which future agents can still choose well.

From what you describe, I think Julie and Mark did wrong, but not in the way people usually imagine: not because sex between siblings is inherently impure or disgusting, and not because pregnancy or disease was a risk, since the pill and the condom were used.

The main problem is the sibling relationship itself. It is not just a bond between two individuals, but a lifelong relationship with certain roles, expectations and often unequal power. Even if there was no coercion and both were adults, it is hard to know whether consent was entirely free or influenced by family dynamics. Nor does pleasure or the feeling of being closer prove that the relationship is healthy; people can feel closer after a transgression of boundaries.

Keeping the matter secret is also dangerous. A secret that cannot be openly integrated can isolate them, make the relationship fragile and create a burden that neither can easily put down. Since the act changes the relationship in ways that cannot be fully undone, it is not a small matter.

I am fairly confident in this judgment, but not certain. If there had been any coercion, abuse, dependency or unequal power, I would judge it much more seriously. As it is, I do not think they are wicked people or that the matter is irredeemable; but I think it was a mistake, and that the secret should no longer be kept between them.

**Eulogy**

My dear family and friends,

Thank you for being here to honor my father. His death last week has left a great void, but it has also brought up many complicated feelings.

For much of my childhood, our home was shaped by his drinking and by the fear of his anger. He hit us, and I do not want to pretend today that this did not happen. Alcoholism took much from our family: peace, trust, and many moments that should have been spent in safety and joy. I do not have to hide this pain in order to honor my father.

At the same time, I do not want to reduce his whole life to his illness. [Insert a specific memory here, if you wish.] There were also [insert other memories or qualities, if you wish]. I do not have to find a perfect balance between love and anger, or between the good and the bad. Both can remain true.

Today I do not want to judge him, nor to defend him. I want to speak the truth about what he was: a man who struggled, who hurt us, and who was not perfect. I carry his example, for better and worse, into my own life. I am grateful for [names or people] who supported us when we needed help.

I will not erase the pain he caused. But I will also not let it consume my whole life. May he rest in peace, and may we who loved him find peace in our own healing.

Thank you.

---
